newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong's Tsang says he's no puppet of China.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong's Tsang says he's no puppet of China.

text.p: Hong Kong's Financial Secretary rejected suggestions on Thursday that he was Beijing's puppet in formulating his budget for the financial year straddling the colony's return to China.
Donald Tsang received a public pummelling on government radio for drafting what many in Hong Kong regarded as a miserly budget.
He denied allegations the government was tight-fisted with welfare spending, despite coffers overflowing with cash.

In his budget speech on Wednesday, Tsang reported a HK$15.1 billion ($1.96 billion) budget surplus and forecast more to come. But he resisted the temptation to proffer tax cuts for 1997/98 -- which covers the year when British rule ends at midnight on June 30.
Tsang had to contend with China breathing down his neck when he drafted his budget -- the first time Beijing was consulted as Hong Kong crunched its numbers.
But the Financial Secretary, known for his flamboyant bow-ties and outspoken views, shrugged off any suggestion that he danced to China's tune.
"I do not consider myself a puppet. I am just being a realist," he told a Radio Hong Kong phone-in programme.
"We are working closely with the Chinese side. They had been commenting, they had been watching. And all I can say is this is very much our own budget too, following our own discipline."

China's insistence that it be involved in drawing up the budget, even before the handover, and past criticism by Chinese officials of rising welfare spending in the territory, raised fears in Hong Kong that its budget would be dictated by Beijing.
But Tsang has insisted in recent days that Chinese participation had not swayed Hong Kong from its budgetary principles.
Years of strict controls on government spending -- spending is not permitted to exceed economic growth -- have left Hong Kong, a community of 6.3 million people, awash with cash.

It approaches the handover with reserves in the bank in excess of HK$330 billion ($42.3 billion), a sum Tsang's predecessor later said he regretted, describing it as "the greatest dowry since Cleopatra".
Demands for a better quality of life have ballooned.
Hong Kong's per capita gross domestic product of US$24,500 now exceeds Britain's but the safety net for the disadvantaged, while among the most extensive in Asia, is rudimentary.
Tsang said welfare spending, particularly on the elderly, "has increased by 88 percent over the past five years".
"And even this year, we are proposing an increase in welfare spending of 9.4 percent," he said.
Tsang described the cash pile as a surplus "for a very rainy day" and had no intention of eating into Hong Kong's massive savings.
Hong Kong approaches the handover with many concerns -- mainly linked to politics and China's plans to roll back civil liberties -- but economic anxiety is not among the worries.
A long-term study conducted by Hong Kong Baptist University of the transition showed growing prosperity had buoyed confidence in the face of the momentous change ahead.

"People are already politically pessimistic. They are already politically sensitive. It is the economic performance that holds them together," said Michael DeGolyer, director of the transitional project.
An opinion poll released by the project on Thursday found 62 percent of 546 respondents were optimistic about Hong Kong's future under the Chinese flag, he said. ($1 = HK$7.8)
